title: How do you centralize logs across many services/containers (ELK/EFK, Loki), and how do you trace a single request end-to-end across services (correlation/trace ID propagation, OpenTelemetry, Jaeger/Zipkin)?
shortTitle: Centralizing logs across many services/containers (ELK/EFK, Loki) and tracing a single request end-to-end (correlation ID, OpenTelemetry, Jaeger/Zipkin)
keyPoints: Centralized logging means every service writes structured JSON logs to stdout and a collector ships them to one searchable store
ELK (Elasticsearch + Logstash + Kibana) gives rich full-text search; EFK swaps in Fluentd/Fluent Bit for Kubernetes
Loki indexes only labels (service, namespace) and stores log bodies compressed, making it cheaper but less suited to arbitrary text search
Distributed tracing uses a trace ID generated at the edge and propagated via W3C traceparent headers through every service call
OpenTelemetry is the vendor-neutral standard for auto-instrumentation; Jaeger and Zipkin store and visualize traces
Correlation: put the trace ID into the MDC so every log line carries it, enabling pivot from trace to logs instantly

s1_definition.oneliner: Ship every service's structured logs to one searchable store, and stamp every request with a propagated trace ID so you can reconstruct its whole cross-service journey.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Centralized logging** means every service writes structured JSON logs to stdout, a collector on each node ships them to a single store, and you query all logs in one place
- **ELK** (Elasticsearch + Logstash + Kibana) indexes full log content for rich text search; **EFK** swaps in Fluentd/Fluent Bit as the shipper
- **Loki** indexes only a small set of labels and stores log bodies compressed, queried with LogQL in Grafana, making it far cheaper at scale
- **Distributed tracing** follows a single request across services by generating a trace ID at the edge and propagating it through every call via W3C traceparent headers
- **OpenTelemetry** is the vendor-neutral instrumentation standard; **Jaeger** and **Zipkin** store and visualize the span waterfall
s1_definition.analogy: When a transfer from Rajesh SAV2001 to Priya CUR3001 passes through five different departments at the National Bank of India, each department used to keep its own private diary. Centralized logging is like photocopying every diary entry and filing it in one central records room that anyone can search instantly. Distributed tracing adds a single case number stamped on the transfer form the moment it enters the building, and every department writes that same case number in its diary. Now the investigator searches the central room for one case number and instantly sees the complete journey across all five departments in order.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Centralizing logs means every service writes structured JSON to stdout, a collector like Fluent Bit running as a DaemonSet tails those logs, enriches them with pod metadata, and ships them to one searchable store. ELK indexes the full content for rich text search but is storage-heavy. Loki takes a cheaper approach by indexing only labels and compressing the log bodies, queried with LogQL in Grafana. The goal is always the same: one place to search instead of logging into every host.

Tracing a single request end-to-end is solved by trace context propagation. At the edge, the API gateway generates a unique trace ID, each unit of work becomes a span, and the crucial step is propagation through the W3C `traceparent` header when one service calls another. OpenTelemetry auto-instruments incoming and outgoing calls, and Jaeger or Zipkin draw the waterfall showing each service's duration and errors.

The two come together through correlation. Putting the trace ID into the MDC means every log line carries it, so from a trace in Jaeger you can pivot straight to the logs filtered by that exact trace ID. In the National Bank of India project, a transfer from Rajesh's SAV2001 to Priya's CUR3001 passed through four services. When a transfer failed intermittently, the team searched the central log store for one trace ID and instantly saw the complete ordered journey, while the trace waterfall showed the fraud service was the slow hop.

Remember one sentence: centralized structured logs give you one place to look, and a propagated trace ID gives you the thread that stitches a single request's whole cross-service journey together.
